## In 60 seconds

Most failures of AI in practice start outside the model. A file header with the wrong gain changes every
amplitude; labels from experts who disagree cap what any model can score; a released table can identify the
people in it; a dataset changes without its name changing; a model shrunk to fit a wearable is a different
model. This module turns each of these into something you can compute and check: the header conversion
$v = (d - b)/g$ [@wfdbheader], the accuracy of a majority of labellers, the re-identification risk $1/f$ of a
record that shares its values with $f - 1$ others [@eleman2008], a checksum manifest that fingerprints a dataset
version [@wilkinson2016], the step size and noise of integer quantization [@jacob2018quant; @wu2020int8], and a
model card that records all of it [@mitchell2019modelcards; @gebru2018datasheets].

## From the field

- **Labels are measurements too.** In the PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2017, disagreement between experts was high
  enough that the organizers relabelled contentious recordings during the competition [@clifford2017]. PTB-XL
  records were annotated by up to two cardiologists, and the database ships diagnosis likelihoods and manually
  annotated signal properties with the labels [@wagner2020]; a well-known single-lead study used a test set annotated by a consensus
  committee of cardiologists [@hannun2019].
- **The ECG itself can identify a person.** A deep network trained on about 40,000 patients identified
  individuals from their ECGs with 94.56% accuracy; accuracy varied by heart condition, for example 78.54% for
  patients with premature ventricular contractions [@ghazarian2021].
- **De-identification of text is a model to validate.** A Stanford pipeline that finds and replaces protected
  health information in radiology reports reached F1 scores of 97.9 on reports from a known institution and 99.6
  from a new one [@chambon2023].
- **Small devices.** A 2,680-parameter arrhythmia network was pruned, quantized and run on a microcontroller with
  64 KB of memory; its accuracy on MIT-BIH was 98.07% overall but 80.73% when evaluated patient-independently at
  record level [@huang2026edgeecg], a reminder that the split decides the number (m35). Distilling a larger
  network into a smaller one raised the F-score after quantization from 0.779 to 0.828 in an AF-detection study
  on a low-power chip [@faraone2021].
- **Integer arithmetic (NVIDIA).** An NVIDIA study reviewed the choices behind integer quantization and reported
  an 8-bit workflow that kept accuracy within 1% of the floating-point baseline on all the vision, speech and
  language networks it studied [@wu2020int8].
- **Documentation (Stanford).** A Stanford-led analysis of 32,111 model cards on Hugging Face found that
  sections on limitations, evaluation and environmental impact were filled in least often, and training details
  most consistently [@liang2024modelcards].

## Derivations

### Data formats: units live in the header

A WFDB record stores integers $d$ in analog-to-digital converter units (adu); its header gives the gain $g$ in adu
per physical unit and the baseline $b$, the stored value that means zero [@wfdbheader]. The physical value is

$$
v = \frac{d - b}{g}, \qquad \lvert v_{\text{stored}} - v \rvert \le \frac{1}{2g}
$$ {#eq-m47-adu}

where the bound is the rounding error when a physical signal is written as integers. The format documentation
says that a missing gain means the amplitude is uncalibrated and that 200 adu per physical unit may be assumed,
and that missing units may be taken as millivolts [@wfdbpyconvert]: a file with a wrong or missing header still
opens. In lab part A a header claiming gain 1000 instead of 200 shrank every
amplitude five-fold, and one claiming 500 instead of 250 samples per second doubled every heart rate. An audit
that only learned the 1st to 99th percentiles of R amplitude and heart rate from training data flagged all 30
recordings in each case and 0–3% of correct ones.

**Key takeaways**

- Read the header before the signal: rate, gain, baseline and units decide every later number.
- Audit new data against ranges learned from training data; a flag means "look", not "reject".
- A model whose features are ratios (for example RR variability) can hide a wrong sampling rate.

### Labels: what a majority vote can fix

If each of $m$ labellers (odd $m$) is right with probability $p$, independently, the majority is right with
probability

$$
P_{\text{maj}}(m, p) = \sum_{j=(m+1)/2}^{m} \binom{m}{j}\, p^{j} (1 - p)^{m-j}
$$ {#eq-m47-majority}

which grows toward 1 with $m$ when $p > 0.5$. Real labellers share hard cases, and a vote cannot fix a shared
mistake. In lab part C, labellers who were right 79% of the time gave a seven-labeller majority of 0.96 when
independent, but 0.91 when 20% of recordings were hard for everyone. Agreement is measured with Cohen's
kappa ([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-kappa)), and noisy reference labels cap the accuracy you can
measure ([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-label-ceiling)): a model that is right 95% of the time scored
0.76 against one labeller in the lab.

**Key takeaways**

- Votes fix independent errors, not shared ones; adjudicate hard cases.
- Report how labels were made: who, how many, agreement, and what was done with disagreement.
- Keep label versions; relabelling changes every reported metric [@clifford2017].

### De-identification and re-identification risk

Fields such as age, sex, region and procedure date are quasi-identifiers: harmless alone, identifying together.
Group the records that share all released quasi-identifier values; record $i$ is in a group of size $f_i$.
Someone who knows a person's values, and that the person is in the data, picks the right record with probability
$1/f_i$. Over a table of $n$ records in $J$ groups,

$$
r_i = \frac{1}{f_i}, \qquad R_{\max} = \frac{1}{\min_i f_i} = \frac{1}{k}, \qquad
\bar R = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{f_i} = \frac{J}{n}
$$ {#eq-m47-risk}

where $k$ is the smallest group size: the table is $k$-anonymous [@eleman2008]. In a synthetic registry of 5,000
procedures (lab part D), 99.6% of records were unique with age, sex, device, region and procedure day released.
Reaching $k = 5$ took dropping the date and the region, ten-year age groups, and grouping the youngest and oldest
ages. In the United States, HIPAA allows de-identification by expert determination of very small risk or by the
Safe Harbor method, which removes a list of identifier types (18 types) and requires no actual knowledge that
the rest identifies someone [@hhsdeid; @hhsdeidworkshop]. HHS guidance cites estimates that date of birth, sex
and five-digit ZIP code together are unique for over half of US residents [@hhsdeid].

::: {.demo #m47-d2 badge="simulation"}
```{=html}
<div id="m47-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m47-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m47-d2-reidentification.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: a synthetic registry of 2,000 procedures from a fixed seed: age from a normal distribution (mean 65,
  standard deviation 12 years, limited to 18–95), a sex code, 30 region codes used unevenly (weights 1, 1/2, …,
  1/30), a procedure day of one year and three device models in shares 60%, 30% and 10%. All distributions are illustrative; there are no real people.
- Risk follows @eq-m47-risk for an attacker who knows the person is in the registry; the JavaScript is tested
  against `epml.deploy`.
- What would change the result: a larger registry (more records share values), an attacker who does not know who
  is included (lower risk), outside data that adds fields, and the waveforms themselves, which can identify
  people [@ghazarian2021].
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Count unique records before release; most risk sits in rare combinations and extreme values.
- Coarsening trades detail for privacy; decide which fields the analysis really needs.
- Table de-identification does not cover waveforms or free text; each needs its own assessment [@chambon2023].

### Versions: a fingerprint for every dataset

A SHA-256 checksum changes when any bit of a file changes. A manifest lists the checksum of every file, and the
checksum of the manifest identifies the whole dataset version. This course pins the checksum lists of the
PhysioNet databases it downloads in `data/registry.json`. In lab part B flipping one bit in one signal file
changed the dataset version and named the file. Persistent identifiers and rich metadata make data findable and
reusable by machines as well as people [@wilkinson2016].

**Key takeaways**

- Record the data version next to every result, model and model card.
- Verify downloads against published checksums; pin the list itself.

### Deployment: integer quantization

Quantization stores a real value $r$ as an integer $q$ with a scale $S$ and zero point $Z$ [@jacob2018quant]:

$$
r = S\,(q - Z), \qquad S = \frac{r_{\max} - r_{\min}}{q_{\max} - q_{\min}}, \qquad
Z = q_{\min} - \operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{r_{\min}}{S}\right)
$$ {#eq-m47-affine}

where $[r_{\min}, r_{\max}]$ is the chosen range (widened to include 0, so that zero is exact) and
$[q_{\min}, q_{\max}]$ the integer range, for example 0 to 255 for 8 bits. With 8-bit weights and activations the
memory is close to a quarter of 32-bit floating point [@jacob2018quant]. Inside the range the rounding error is
spread evenly over one step, so

$$
\sigma_e^2 = \frac{S^2}{12}, \qquad
\mathrm{SQNR} = 10 \log_{10} \frac{\overline{x^2}}{S^2/12}\ \text{dB} \;\approx\; 6.02\,b + 1.76\ \text{dB for a full-scale sine}
$$ {#eq-m47-qnoise}

where SQNR is the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio, $\overline{x^2}$ the mean square of the signal and $b$ the
number of bits; each extra bit adds about 6 dB. A range wider than the signal wastes levels: in lab part E an
8-bit beat had an SQNR of 44 dB over its own range and 26 dB over a fixed ±5 mV range. For the m46 network, 8-bit
weights left the AUC unchanged (0.961) at a quarter of the size; 4-bit weights changed 2.4% of decisions with one
scale per tensor and 1.2% with one scale per hidden unit.

::: {.demo #m47-d1 badge="approximate model"}
```{=html}
<div id="m47-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m47-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m47-d1-quantization.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: the synthetic m37 beat (Gaussian waves, illustrative amplitudes) at 250 samples per second, quantized
  with @eq-m47-affine over its own range or over a fixed ±5 mV range (an illustrative value, not a device
  specification). The quantizer is tested against `epml.deploy`.
- The predicted line uses the uniform-noise model of @eq-m47-qnoise; it ignores that at very few bits the
  rounding error follows the signal's shape and is no longer uniform, so measurement and prediction differ there.
- What would change the result: noise already in the signal (which dithers the rounding), clipping when the range
  is too narrow, and the analog front end (m14).
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Each bit is worth about 6 dB; choosing the range well is worth as much as several bits.
- One scale per output channel helps when weights in different rows have different ranges.
- A quantized model is a new model: test it on the same data and subgroups as the original (m45, m46).

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where these issues arise in EP.** ECGs and electrograms move from recording systems into hospital archives and
research databases, often through exports that carry their own headers and units. AI-ECG and EP datasets are
labelled by clinicians who disagree on hard cases [@clifford2017; @wagner2020]. Multicentre projects share data
or train where the data live (federated learning, m45). Detection algorithms increasingly run on wearables and
implants with little memory [@huang2026edgeecg; @faraone2021].

**What the evidence is.** The studies here describe datasets, methods and engineering results. None shows how
data-pipeline errors, label quality or quantization change patient outcomes; the examples in this module are
synthetic.

**What a reader should ask:**

- **Data.** Which database version, sampling rate, gain and units? How were labels made and adjudicated?
- **Privacy.** How was the data de-identified, and is the waveform itself considered identifying
  [@ghazarian2021]?
- **Deployment.** Was the model evaluated in the form that runs on the device, quantized and on the device's
  own recordings?

## How experts think

Before trusting a dataset or a deployed model, ask:

1. **What exactly is in the files?** Sampling rate, gain, baseline, units, filters, and the database
   version (@eq-m47-adu).
2. **Where do the labels come from?** Number of labellers, agreement, adjudication and relabelling, as
   in @eq-m47-majority and the kappa of [m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-kappa).
3. **Who could be identified, and how?** Class sizes, rare values, waveforms and text (@eq-m47-risk).
4. **Can I reproduce this number?** Data version, code version, model checksum.
5. **Is the deployed model the tested model?** Quantization, device, input pipeline
   (@eq-m47-affine and @eq-m47-qnoise).

One sentence to keep: **every number about a model is also a number about its data pipeline; write both down.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Header conversion (@eq-m47-adu) | $v = (d - b)/g$; rounding error at most $1/(2g)$ |
| Majority of $m$ labellers (@eq-m47-majority) | $\sum_{j=(m+1)/2}^{m}\binom{m}{j}p^j(1-p)^{m-j}$; for $m = 3$: $3p^2 - 2p^3$ |
| Re-identification risk (@eq-m47-risk) | $r_i = 1/f_i$; largest $1/k$; average $J/n$ |
| Affine quantization (@eq-m47-affine) | $r = S(q - Z)$, $S = (r_{\max} - r_{\min})/(q_{\max} - q_{\min})$ |
| Quantization noise (@eq-m47-qnoise) | $\sigma_e^2 = S^2/12$; about 6 dB per bit |

**Sources in this module**

| Source | What it adds | Kind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| @wagner2020, @clifford2017, @hannun2019 | How public and published ECG datasets were labelled | Dataset papers and a retrospective study |
| @ghazarian2021 | Re-identification of patients from ECGs | Method study |
| @chambon2023 | De-identification of report text (Stanford) | Retrospective method study |
| @huang2026edgeecg, @faraone2021 | Arrhythmia models on microcontrollers | Method studies |
| @jacob2018quant, @wu2020int8 | Integer quantization (Google; NVIDIA) | Method studies |
| @mitchell2019modelcards, @gebru2018datasheets, @liang2024modelcards | Model cards, datasheets, and how cards are filled in (Stanford) | Proposals and an analysis |

**Rules of thumb**

- Audit headers and amplitudes on every new data source.
- Count unique records before any release; remember waveforms and free text.
- Quantize, then retest on the same data and subgroups; record checksums in the model card.

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. A model trained on one database scores poorly on another. Before blaming the model, what do you check?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The data pipeline: sampling rate, gain, baseline and units in the headers (@eq-m47-adu), filters, lead
placement, and how labels were made. Compare amplitude and heart-rate distributions with the training data; a
wrong header or a different filter can look like a model failure [@wfdbheader].

</details>

**Q2. Why does a missing gain in a WFDB header matter?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The amplitude is then uncalibrated, and a default of 200 adu per physical unit may be assumed [@wfdbpyconvert],
so the file opens without an error but every amplitude may be wrong by a constant factor. Amplitude-based features and models change; ratio
features may not, which hides the problem.

</details>

**Q3. You have three labellers who are each right 80% of the time. How accurate is their majority?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$3p^2 - 2p^3 = 0.896$ if their errors are independent (@eq-m47-majority). If they share hard cases, less: the vote
cannot fix a mistake everyone makes. Measure agreement with kappa
([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-kappa)) and adjudicate disagreements.

</details>

**Q4. Why can't you measure a model's accuracy above the accuracy of its labels?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Against labels that are wrong at rate $\epsilon$, a model with true accuracy $a$ scores
$a(1 - \epsilon) + (1 - a)\epsilon$ if the errors are independent
([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-label-ceiling)). A perfect model scores $1 - \epsilon$. Better reference labels (consensus, adjudication [@hannun2019]) raise the ceiling.

</details>

**Q5. What is a quasi-identifier, and how do you measure the risk it creates?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A field that identifies people only in combination, such as age, sex, region or a procedure date. Group records
by their released values; a record in a group of $f$ has risk $1/f$ against someone who knows the person is in the
data, the table's largest risk is $1/k$ and the average is groups over records (@eq-m47-risk) [@eleman2008].

</details>

**Q6. A table has been de-identified. Can you release the ECG waveforms with it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Not without a separate assessment: deep networks have identified people from their ECGs with high accuracy
[@ghazarian2021]. Waveforms and free-text reports need their own de-identification and often a data-use
agreement; text de-identification tools are models with their own error rates [@chambon2023].

</details>

**Q7. How do you know two teams used the same dataset?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Compare checksum manifests, or a single identifier computed from the manifest, not file names or dataset names.
Verify downloads against the publisher's checksum list and pin that list; record the version with every result
[@wilkinson2016].

</details>

**Q8. Explain scale and zero point in 8-bit quantization.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A real value is stored as $r = S(q - Z)$ (@eq-m47-affine) [@jacob2018quant]: $S$ maps one integer step to a real
step, and $Z$ is the integer that represents real zero exactly. The range is chosen from the data or a calibration
set; values outside it are clipped.

</details>

**Q9. How much does one extra bit improve the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

About 6 dB: the step halves, so the noise variance $S^2/12$ falls four-fold (@eq-m47-qnoise). For a full-scale
sine the SQNR is about $6.02b + 1.76$ dB. A range much wider than the signal costs the same as losing bits.

</details>

**Q10. A model is quantized to 8 bits for a wearable. What do you test before deployment?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The quantized model on the same test data and subgroups as the original: discrimination, calibration, decision
changes at the operating threshold, and performance on recordings from the device itself. An 8-bit workflow can
stay within 1% of floating-point accuracy [@wu2020int8], but that is a result to confirm, not assume; treat it as a
model change (m45).

</details>

**Q11. What goes into a model card for an AI-ECG model?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Intended use and out-of-scope uses, training and evaluation data with versions, metrics overall and by group with
intervals, limitations, and the checksum of the deployed weights [@mitchell2019modelcards]. A datasheet does the
same for the data [@gebru2018datasheets]. Limitations and evaluation are the sections most often left empty
[@liang2024modelcards].

</details>

**Q12. A paper reports 98% accuracy for an arrhythmia model on a microcontroller. What do you ask?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

How the data were split. In one study accuracy was 98.07% overall but 80.73% when evaluated patient-independently
at record level [@huang2026edgeecg]. Also: which classes, which database, and whether the number is for the
quantized model running on the device.

</details>

## Code lab

The lab builds each check on synthetic data and then audits real PhysioNet headers.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Units in WFDB headers and an audit that catches header mistakes (@eq-m47-adu) | synthetic ECGs |
| B | Checksums, a manifest and a dataset version | synthetic files |
| C | Several labellers, majority votes and agreement (@eq-m47-majority) | synthetic labels |
| D | Re-identification risk and coarsening (@eq-m47-risk) | synthetic registry |
| E | Quantizing inputs and weights (@eq-m47-affine, @eq-m47-qnoise) | synthetic beats |
| F | A model card generated from the lab's own results | parts B and E |
| G | Real headers, label-quality fields and an amplitude audit across databases | PTB-XL and Challenge 2017 (download) |
| H | Optional: dynamic int8 quantization in PyTorch | synthetic beats |

- **Python notebook:**
  [labs/python/m47_lab.ipynb]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m47_lab.ipynb).
  Run it from the course repository after `pip install -r requirements.txt`, or
  [open it in Google Colab]({{< var repo.colab >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m47_lab.ipynb).
- **Data for part G:** PTB-XL 1.0.3 [@wagner2020] (Creative Commons Attribution 4.0) and the PhysioNet/CinC
  Challenge 2017 training set [@cinc2017data; @clifford2017] (Open Data Commons Attribution v1.0); only header
  files, the PTB-XL metadata table and a few recordings are downloaded, checked against the published SHA-256
  lists, and the part is skipped without internet access.
- **Part H** runs only if PyTorch is installed.

Each part ends with **checks**: lines that pass with the code as given. If you change something
and a check fails, that is information, not an error to hide.

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. A stored value is 450 adu, the baseline 50 adu and the gain 200 adu/mV. What is the voltage?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$(450 - 50)/200 = 2$ mV (@eq-m47-adu).

</details>

**S2. Three independent labellers are each right 90% of the time. How often is their majority right?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$3(0.81) - 2(0.729) = 0.972$ (@eq-m47-majority).

</details>

**S3. A table of 1,000 records falls into 250 groups, the smallest with 2 records. What are the largest and
average risks?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Largest $1/2 = 0.5$; average $250/1000 = 0.25$ (@eq-m47-risk).

</details>

**S4. An 8-bit unsigned quantizer covers −1 to 3. What are the scale and zero point?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$S = 4/255 \approx 0.0157$ and $Z = 0 - \operatorname{round}(-1/S) = 64$ (@eq-m47-affine).

</details>

**S5. Going from 8 to 12 bits over the same range improves SQNR by about how much?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

About $4 \times 6 = 24$ dB (@eq-m47-qnoise).

</details>

**S6. True or false: if a file opens without an error, its units are right.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

False. A missing or wrong gain still gives a readable file, with every amplitude scaled (lab part A).

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **PTB-XL's structure.** Wagner and colleagues describe how records, labels, metadata and the recommended folds
  fit together [@wagner2020; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7248071/)]. This module:
  data formats and labels.
- **k-anonymity in practice.** El Emam and Dankar compare the re-identification risk and information loss of
  k-anonymity and its variants on large health data sets [@eleman2008;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2528029/)]. This module: re-identification risk.
- **De-identifying report text.** Chambon and colleagues describe a pipeline that detects protected health
  information and replaces it with realistic surrogates [@chambon2023;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9846681/)]. This module: de-identification.
